title: Runtime LTS (Private/VPC/On‑Prem) Upgrade & Rollback Guide
author: Kira Thompson
body:
## Purpose
This guide explains how to upgrade and roll back **Redwood Serving Runtime** in **Private** deployments (VPC and on‑prem) when using the **Runtime LTS channel**. It is written for platform/infra teams operating Redwood Private in production.

This guide covers:
- Pinning to specific LTS artifacts ("slower-change" runtime line)
- Supported upgrade paths within an LTS line
- Safe rollback procedures, including required validation
- What to do if your deployment includes multiple regions / multi‑cluster

Out of scope:
- Non-runtime components (control plane, console, telemetry stack) unless needed for compatibility
- Feature upgrades across non‑LTS (standard) runtime trains

---

## Audience
- Private deployment operators (Kubernetes and installer-based)
- SRE/on-call responsible for change windows and rollback decisions
- Security/compliance reviewers validating provenance/signing requirements

---

## Definitions & versioning
### Runtime LTS version format
We publish Runtime LTS artifacts with an LTS line and patch number:
- **LTS line**: `runtime-1.20-lts`
- **Patch releases**: `runtime-1.20-lts.0`, `runtime-1.20-lts.1`, ...

Notes:
- **Only patch releases** ship on an LTS line. No new features; changes are limited to security fixes, correctness fixes, stability fixes, and narrowly scoped performance/regression fixes per the backport policy.
- Each patch includes enterprise-oriented release notes (risk level, behavior changes, known issues, mitigations).

### Artifact types (Private)
Depending on your deployment mode, you will consume one or more of:
- Container images (runtime data plane)
- Helm chart values (runtime deployment configuration)
- Installer bundle references (for air‑gapped / offline on‑prem)
- Signed provenance / attestations for runtime artifacts

---

## Compatibility and support policy (Private)
### Supported upgrade paths
**Supported**:
1) **Within an LTS line (recommended)**
   - `runtime-1.20-lts.0` → `runtime-1.20-lts.1` → `runtime-1.20-lts.2` …
   - You may skip patches (e.g., `.0` → `.2`) if release notes do not require intermediate steps.

2) **Standard → LTS (same minor), with validation**
   - Example: `runtime-1.20.x` (standard channel) → `runtime-1.20-lts.0`
   - This is allowed only when the LTS line is cut from the same minor series and compatibility gates pass.

**Not supported (without an exception)**:
- Cross-minor upgrades between LTS lines (e.g., `runtime-1.20-lts.*` → `runtime-1.21-lts.*`) in a single step. Treat this as a **normal runtime minor upgrade** with a dedicated plan.
- Downgrades across LTS lines (e.g., `runtime-1.21-lts.*` → `runtime-1.20-lts.*`) unless Redwood Support explicitly approves (data plane behavior and scheduler semantics may not be backward-compatible).

### Control plane compatibility
Runtime LTS is intended to be **control-plane compatible** with the same Private release family used during the LTS pilot.

Operational rule:
- If your Private control plane is older than the minimum required by a given LTS patch (called out in release notes), upgrade the control plane first.

What to check before upgrading runtime:
- Authentication/authorization compatibility (mTLS, token validation)
- Telemetry/exporter compatibility (metrics names may be additive; deprecations will be flagged)
- Config schema compatibility for runtime deployment values

---

## Where to find LTS artifacts
Your Redwood account team provides a Private artifact registry location and access method. In general:
- **Online (VPC/Kubernetes)**: pull from Redwood-provided OCI registry endpoint(s)
- **Air-gapped on‑prem**: download a signed artifact bundle and import into your internal registry

Always verify:
- Artifact digest (SHA) matches the release notes
- Signing/provenance attestation is present and valid
- The artifact tag matches the intended LTS patch (avoid floating tags like `latest`)

---

## Version pinning (required)
### Why pinning is required for LTS
LTS is designed to reduce operational churn. Pinning ensures:
- Change windows remain deterministic
- Rollback is possible to a known-good digest
- Audit evidence can tie deployed bits to a specific signed release

### Pinning guidance
Pin **by explicit version** and prefer pinning **by digest** when your tooling supports it.

Required:
- Use an explicit runtime image tag `runtime-<minor>-lts.<patch>`.
- Record the **image digest** in your change record.

Recommended:
- Keep a "last-known-good" runtime image reference stored in your deployment repo (GitOps) and in your change ticket.

Anti-patterns:
- Do not deploy LTS using floating tags (`stable`, `lts`, `prod`) unless the tag is additionally constrained by digest.
- Do not rely on implicit upgrades performed by a periodic sync job.

---

## Pre-upgrade checklist (Private)
Complete these before any production runtime LTS upgrade:

1) **Read the LTS patch release notes**
   - Confirm stated risk level (Low/Medium/High)
   - Note any behavior changes, known issues, mitigations
   - Note required config changes (if any)

2) **Confirm your rollback target**
   - Identify currently running runtime version + image digest
   - Ensure the previous image is still available in your registry

3) **Change window + comms**
   - Confirm maintenance window and paging coverage
   - Confirm go/no-go owner (SRE or platform on-call)

4) **Capacity headroom**
   - Ensure you can drain/restart runtime pods without breaching latency/throughput SLOs
   - For multi‑cluster: ensure other regions can absorb load during rollout

5) **Backups / state considerations**
   - Runtime is generally stateless, but validate any local caches and temporary directories are safe to recreate.
   - If your deployment uses persistent volumes for logs/caches, verify cleanup behavior.

6) **Validation plan is ready**
   - Smoke tests: health endpoints, inference requests (streaming and non-streaming)
   - Workload validation: representative prompts, model(s), and concurrency
   - Observability checks: metrics/alerts/dashboards are functioning

---

## Upgrade procedure A: Kubernetes (Helm / GitOps)
This procedure assumes:
- Runtime is deployed in Kubernetes
- You manage runtime settings via Helm values in Git

### Step 1 — Prepare a staged rollout
Recommended rollout pattern:
- Canary (1–5% of traffic) → partial (25–50%) → full

If you do not have traffic splitting at the ingress layer, approximate canary by:
- Deploying a dedicated canary runtime deployment and routing a subset of requests
- Or rolling one node pool / one AZ / one cluster at a time

### Step 2 — Update pinned runtime image
In your Helm values (example keys; use the chart’s actual keys for your deployment):
- Set runtime image tag to `runtime-1.20-lts.1`
- If supported, set runtime image digest to the expected SHA

Also check:
- Any new required env vars or flags called out in the release notes
- Resource requests/limits (some perf fixes may change memory profile; release notes will flag)

### Step 3 — Apply and monitor
Apply the change (GitOps sync or `helm upgrade`) and monitor:
- Pod readiness / startup time
- Error rate (HTTP 5xx / gRPC errors)
- Latency (p95 and p99) and throughput
- GPU utilization, memory (HBM) and OOM events

Canary duration:
- Follow the LTS regression gates doc for minimum canary time. If not specified for your environment, use **at least 60 minutes** of representative traffic.

### Step 4 — Promote to full rollout
Proceed only if:
- No sustained error-rate increase
- No sustained p95/p99 latency regression beyond your configured thresholds
- No increase in crashlooping/evictions

Record:
- Start/end timestamps
- Runtime image tag + digest
- Dashboard links / exported metrics snapshots

---

## Upgrade procedure B: Installer-based Private (VPC/on‑prem)
This procedure assumes you use the Redwood Private installer workflow (including offline/air‑gapped).

### Step 1 — Acquire the LTS artifact bundle (if applicable)
For offline installs:
- Download the runtime LTS bundle for `runtime-1.20-lts.1`
- Verify signatures/provenance
- Import images to your internal registry

### Step 2 — Pin versions in installer config
Update installer config to:
- Reference the target LTS version explicitly
- Reference exact image digests (recommended)

### Step 3 — Run preflight checks
Run installer preflight and confirm:
- Registry reachability (or internal registry availability)
- Node GPU driver / CUDA compatibility remains within supported bounds
- Disk space (images + logs)
- Time sync (NTP) and cert validity windows

### Step 4 — Execute rolling update
Use a rolling update where possible:
- Drain one runtime node/pod group at a time
- Wait for readiness and health checks before proceeding

### Step 5 — Post-install validation
See the “Validation steps (required)” section below.

---

## Validation steps (required)
Perform these after any LTS upgrade and before declaring success.

### 1) Health and readiness
- Confirm runtime health endpoint returns OK
- Confirm no elevated restarts/crashloops

### 2) Functional inference smoke tests
Run a small suite that reflects your usage:
- Standard completion
- Chat with system+user messages
- Streaming responses
- Tool/function calling (if used)
- Any structured output mode you depend on

Record:
- Request IDs
- Model version(s)
- Any anomalies (timeouts, malformed streaming frames, tool-call parsing)

### 3) Performance sanity checks
Compare against your baseline:
- p95 latency
- p99 latency (important for enterprise SLOs)
- Tokens/sec throughput

Recommended: run the same prompt set at the same concurrency as your last-known-good canary.

### 4) Observability and alerts
Confirm:
- Metrics are scraping successfully
- Logs are flowing to your sink
- Critical alerts are firing correctly (you can run a controlled test if your org allows)

---

## Rollback guide (LTS)
### When to roll back
Roll back if any of the following occur during canary or initial rollout:
- Sustained error-rate increase attributable to runtime
- Sustained p95/p99 regression beyond your thresholds
- Crash loops, GPU OOM, or memory leaks not mitigated by config changes
- Confirmed correctness regression in outputs compared to baseline prompt set

If the issue is security-related and rollback increases exposure, engage Security/Support immediately; do not roll back without an explicit decision.

### Rollback principles
- Roll back to the **last-known-good pinned version** (tag + digest).
- Prefer a single-step rollback (do not “bounce” across multiple versions).
- Preserve evidence: keep logs/metrics from the period where regression occurred.

### Rollback procedure A: Kubernetes
1) Revert Helm values/Git commit to the previous runtime image tag + digest
2) Apply (`helm upgrade` or GitOps sync)
3) Monitor as in the upgrade procedure
4) Validate using the required validation steps
5) Freeze further rollout and open an escalation ticket with:
   - Current and rollback image digests
   - Time window
   - Request IDs and error samples
   - Dashboards

### Rollback procedure B: Installer-based
1) Update installer config to previous runtime image tag + digest
2) Execute rolling rollback
3) Validate using the required validation steps
4) Capture evidence and escalate

---

## Rollback validation (must-pass)
After rollback, confirm:
- Error rate returns to baseline
- p95 and p99 latency return to baseline (or within acceptable variance)
- No new data plane instability (restarts, OOM)
- Key customer workflows are restored (use your smoke suite)

If rollback does not restore baseline:
- Treat as an incident and engage on-call escalation
- Consider whether the issue is upstream (drivers, cluster changes, traffic pattern shift)

---

## Common failure modes & mitigations
### 1) Image pull / registry failures
Symptoms:
- Pods stuck in ImagePullBackOff

Mitigations:
- Confirm registry credentials and network policies
- For offline: confirm bundle import completed and image tags/digests match

### 2) Config schema mismatch
Symptoms:
- Runtime fails to start due to unknown flags or missing required settings

Mitigations:
- Review release notes “Configuration changes”
- Validate chart/installer version supports the runtime config keys

### 3) Latency regression only at p99
Symptoms:
- p95 stable, p99 worsens under load

Mitigations:
- Check for GPU memory pressure and eviction patterns
- Confirm batching/caching settings are unchanged
- Increase canary duration to capture tail behavior
- Escalate with perf traces if available

### 4) Correctness / output diffs
Symptoms:
- Output formatting or tool-calling behavior changes

Mitigations:
- Check release notes for any behavior changes (should be rare in LTS)
- Validate deterministic settings (temperature, top_p) are unchanged
- Roll back if customer impact is confirmed

---

## Multi-cluster / multi-region rollout guidance
Recommended strategy:
1) Staging environment first (if representative)
2) Smallest production region canary
3) One region at a time

Operational note:
- Ensure routing can fail over to a stable region during rollout.
- Ensure you can roll back in one region without forcing rollbacks globally.

---

## Escalation and support
If you hit an upgrade/rollback issue:
- Open a Support escalation (SUP ticket) and include:
  - Deployed version(s) and digests
  - Cluster/region
  - Time window
  - Error samples + request IDs
  - Release notes link for the patch
  - Whether rollback was attempted and outcome

Internal escalation path:
- Private Deployments on-call → Runtime backport owner → Release Engineering (if artifact/pipeline suspected)

---

## Appendix: Change record template (copy/paste)
Use this format in your internal change ticket:
- Change type: Runtime LTS patch upgrade
- Source version (tag + digest):
- Target version (tag + digest):
- Maintenance window:
- Rollout plan: canary duration, regions/clusters order
- Validation steps: smoke suite link, perf baseline link
- Rollback plan: exact pinned target, decision owner
- Evidence links: dashboards, logs, CI/provenance (if applicable)

---

## Appendix: Minimum “must-have” tests for Private operators
If you do not have an existing suite, start with:
- 10–20 representative prompts across your top models
- Concurrency sweep (low, medium, peak)
- Streaming on/off
- Tool-calling path (if applicable)
- 60-minute soak at expected steady-state load

Record and retain results per your internal audit policy.
